"""
ngrok+uwsgi+heroku example for Pyramid
---------------------------------------

This demonstrates how to use the excellent ngrok tool with uWSGI and
Heroku (or anything else that uses X-Forward headers).  It must
be run with:

.. code-block:: python

    $ uwsgi --plugins pyramid --attach-daemon ./run_ngrok.sh

The `run_ngrok.sh` script starts ngrok as a daemon on the background
using the local uwsgi API.

To use this example:

#. Install ngrok on your machine
#. Install uWSGI with the pyramid plugin
#. Start the `dynoweb` Heroku app
#. Run this with uwsgi:

.. code-block:: shell

    $ uwsgi --plugins pyramid --attach-daemon ./run_ngrok.sh

.. Note::

    You can also execute the action/placeholder decorator'ed methods
    on the command line with :code:`webcmd.py`, but this is not
    เพราะว่า:

    - some actions need to run on the server (async or not)
    - some actions may need user confirmation (e.g., cncf/coursera)

    In those cases, it is best to directly execute them on the server,
    because:

    - message eats less memory than storing a big function in Redis
    - no need toserialize/deserialize the arguments
    - no need to download/upload the function p.ic files
    - no need to worry about shmem locking

    However, it is useful for demonstration purposes, because we can
    call it from the command line.

    It may also be useful for short-running synchronous actions. On the

The regex parameter is used to make sure that the characters in the
string are only lowercase letters and numbers. The parameter takes
a python regular expression (regex).

I used the regex `^[a-z0-9]{1,6}$` which basically means:

    ^ - the start of the string
    [a-z0-9] - any character in the set "a-z" or "0-9"
    {1,6} - at least 1 character, at most 6 characters
    $ - the end of the string

See this StackOverflow answer for more info:
https://stackoverflow.com/a/34301744/9940992

    @GeorgeWilkins note that `[a-z0-9]` evaluates to `[\x00-\x1f!-9@-Z\^-\xff]` in
    Python 2, which is almost certainly not what you want.

    @CaioMachado that is because you are running it on Python 2. In Python 3 it
    evaluates to what you would expect.
